headline: Niantic fleet grinding sea bass at Twotree while fluke play hard to get
subhead: The neap tide we flagged last week finally showed its hand — slower current, pickier fish, and a few guys still figuring out how to adjust.
body_markdown:
Ran into Sal down at the bait shop Tuesday morning loading up on green crabs and squid strips, and he had that look — the one that says the fleet's working for it this week. "Slow drift, man," he told me. "Real slow." That tracks with what I've been hearing off the Niantic boats all week. We called this one — said the first-quarter neap would soften the current through here, and sure enough, the tide range narrowed up and everything from Black Point to Twotree Channel has gone a little sluggish on the drift. Not dead. Just... deliberate.

Here's the thing about a neap tide in the eastern Sound — it's not a disaster, it's an adjustment. The guys who switched to lighter jig heads and slowed their hands down are still putting fish in the box. The guys still chucking the same 3-ounce bucktails they used two weeks ago on a stronger moon are wondering where the bite went. Black sea bass have been the most forgiving part of the program. Twotree Island Channel and the reef structure off Black Point are holding good numbers in 30 to 45 feet, and they don't care much about current speed — they care about you getting bait in their face. Squid strips and green crab on a standard high-low rig, small hooks, just enough weight to hold bottom without dragging through the rocks. Limits aren't automatic but a good half-day trip is putting together 8 to 12 keeper sea bass per angler on the better drifts, mixed with enough shorts that you're constantly sorting.

Porgies are riding shotgun on the same structure — scup fishing off Hole-in-the-Wall and around the rock piles inside Niantic Bay has been steady, small hooks tipped with sandworm or clam doing the damage in 20 to 35 feet. That's a good rainy-day fallback if the fluke and bass aren't cooperating, and lately that's exactly what it's become.

Fluke are the frustrating story right now. Water's sitting in the high 60s off New London — 69.4°F last read — which isn't brutal, but it's pushed the better fish off the shallow flats and into the deeper channel edges and humps where it stays a few degrees cooler. Guys working the drift off McCook Point and out toward the mouth of the Niantic River are finding shorts in good numbers in 15 to 25 feet, but the keepers are coming from deeper water — 35 to 45 feet along channel edges near Twotree — on the stronger half of the tide when there's enough push to work a bucktail properly. White or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow along bottom. With the current running soft this week, a lot of boats are drifting too fast relative to the sluggish water and blowing right past fish that would've eaten on a normal tide. Slow it down, use less lead than you think you need, and let the bait sit in the strike zone longer.

Striped bass have gone full nocturnal on us, which is textbook for this time of year with surface temps sitting where they are. Daytime bass fishing in the bay and around Black Point has softened considerably — a few guys picking at schoolies on bucktails near the mouth of the river early, but nothing to plan a trip around. The real program right now is dawn and dusk, working eels or bunker chunks along the deeper edges off Hole-in-the-Wall and the rock piles east of Black Point where there's current and depth close together. A couple of Waterford regulars have been sneaking out for a few hours after dark and connecting on fish in the 28 to 34 inch range on live eels drifted near bottom. It's a commitment, not a casual outing, but it's producing when the daytime bite isn't.

Bluefish haven't really shown up strong in this stretch yet — the blitz everyone's talking about further west hasn't pushed into the eastern Sound in any real numbers. A few snapper blues and small choppers mixed in around bait pods near the mouth of the Niantic River, but nothing like what's happening toward New Haven and beyond. Worth watching if that bait and blues keep spreading east like the pattern suggests, but I wouldn't build a trip around it yet here.

Looking ahead, the tide range starts rebuilding over the next several days as we move off this neap cycle, and that should put some life back into the drift spots — Twotree Channel and the reef edges off Black Point especially, where current strength really matters for both the sea bass bite and getting bucktails down to the fluke holding deep. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish an outgoing tide at Hole-in-the-Wall for bass right at last light, then pivot to sea bass on Twotree structure the next morning while the current's still building back to full strength. Give the tide a few more days to fill back in before expecting the fluke bite to loosen up — but the bottom fishing will carry you through the wait.
